planting.note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before the last frost, since Peppadew is a long-season pepper that needs a head start to fruit before fall; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun only after the soil has warmed and night temperatures stay reliably above 55°F.

directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay warm; Peppadew is the trademarked name for a piquanté pepper discovered as a chance seedling in a South African garden in the 1990s and now grown commercially worldwide for pickling. The plant is a vigorous, sprawling Capsicum baccatum shrub that produces small, round, tomato-shaped fruit that ripens from green through orange to deep red, carrying a sweet-tart flavor with a mild, tingling heat far gentler than most hot peppers. Because it needs a long, warm growing season to size up and color fully, gardeners in shorter-season climates should start seed extra early and expect the first ripe fruit late in the season; in the Gulf South's long summers it has time to produce a heavy crop. Pick fruit once fully colored and pickle or roast to mellow the skin, as Peppadew is traditionally eaten cured rather than fresh off the plant.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Capsicum baccatum
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

common_name: Beck's Big Buck Okra (Texas Heirloom Giant-Pod Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed once soil has warmed to at least 65°F; Beck's Big Buck is a Texas heirloom bred to hold size without turning woody, so it forgives gardeners who cannot harvest every single day.

directions: Soak seed overnight and direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun; Beck's Big Buck is a Texas heirloom prized for pods that stay tender and stringless even when allowed to grow well past the 4-inch mark where most okra varieties turn fibrous, making it far more forgiving for gardeners who cannot check the patch daily during peak summer production. Plants are tall and vigorous, often topping 6 feet by late summer, and keep setting pods heavily through the worst of the Gulf South's heat once regular blackeyed-pea-type production varieties have slowed. Harvest pods at 4–8 inches for the best balance of size and tenderness, and keep picking to encourage continued flowering; a single well-fed row easily supplies a household through the summer for gumbo, frying, and pickling.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Okra Production

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun at or just after the last frost date. Beam's is a distinct, seed-saver-maintained strain of Yellow Pear kept true-to-type through generations of hand selection.

directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Beam's Yellow Pear is a named heirloom strain of the classic yellow pear cherry tomato, kept distinct from the generic commercial Yellow Pear seed line by seed savers who selected it over many generations for productivity and reliable pear-shaped fruit. The small, teardrop-shaped fruits ripen to a bright, glossy yellow and carry the same mild, low-acid, sweet flavor the type is known for, making them a favorite for salads and snacking as well as for gardeners sensitive to more acidic tomatoes. The indeterminate vine is vigorous and needs sturdy staking or caging, setting fruit in long, heavy clusters over a long season. Because it is an open-pollinated heirloom strain, seed can be saved true-to-type from the healthiest, most productive plants for future seasons.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted softwood cuttings in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; twinberry honeysuckle naturally colonizes streambanks and moist woodland edges and establishes best where it gets consistent soil moisture while young.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where twinberry honeysuckle naturalizes readily along stream edges and under an open woodland canopy across its wide native range from Alaska south through the Pacific Northwest and Rockies. In spring the shrub bears small, paired, tubular yellow flowers tinged with red, followed in summer by shiny black berries held in pairs against a showy pair of deep red bracts — an unmistakable, almost theatrical fruit display that gives the plant its common name. The berries are bitter and unpalatable to people but are readily eaten by robins, waxwings, and other songbirds, and the shrub's dense, arching form provides valuable cover for nesting birds. It tolerates wet soil better than most shrubs sold for shade, making it a strong choice for the damp, low-light corners of a woodland or rain garden where few other flowering shrubs thrive.

common_name: Golden Drops (Lamb's Tail, Oppositeleaf Golden Stonecrop)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; golden drops is native to shaded, moist rock crevices in the Caucasus mountains and does best tucked into a shaded stone wall, crevice garden, or the north side of a rock garden where its roots stay cool and its foliage stays out of hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in gritty, well-drained but moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade, ideally tucked into a shaded rock crevice or stone wall where its roots stay cool; golden drops forms a low, spreading mat of glossy, fleshy, scalloped evergreen leaves that give it a succulent, almost jade-plant-like texture unusual among shade perennials. In late spring, arching sprays of small, star-shaped, bright yellow flowers cascade from the foliage like tiny drooping chains, giving rise to both of its common names. It spreads slowly by short offsets and self-sown seedlings without becoming invasive, making it easy to control in a small shaded rockery or trough garden. It resents waterlogged winter soil far more than drought, so good drainage matters more than rich fertility — a lean, gritty planting mix mimicking its native mountain crevices suits it best.
